The state's Supreme Court is expected to review hundreds of cases before Newsom's clemency would be official.

item.title: Bill Paxton's son takes on Western role late father never got to play: 'I could literally hear my dad'
item.description: James Paxton steps into the Western role his late father Bill Paxton was cast in over 30 years ago, calling the film a "conduit" to connect with him.
item.content:encoded:
Bill Paxton's son, James Paxton, is carrying on his late father's legacy by taking on a Western role that the "Twister" star was originally set to play more than 30 years ago.

In 1991, Bill was cast alongside Malcolm McDowell in the Western comedy drama "Last Train to Fortune," but the project stalled following original director Lindsay Anderson’s death in 1994. "Last Train to Fortune" spent decades trapped in development but efforts to revive the movie were gaining momentum again in 2017 when Bill unexpectedly died, leaving the role that would ultimately be played by James.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, James, 32, opened up about how the project became a deeply personal way to reconnect with Bill, who passed away in February 2017 following heart surgery.

'DEADPOOL' STAR ROB DELANEY REVEALS HOW LOSING 2-YEAR-OLD SON CHANGED HIS APPROACH TO FAME

"When you lose somebody, such a close loved one, you often look for ways to still connect to them," James said.

"And that can take all manner of forms and paths and shapes," he continued. "For me, I recognized immediately that this was the kind of project that I could literally hear my dad in my head the whole time. You know, if I needed any guidance or any motivation, or I had any questions, I knew that he would kind of — he would be right there with me, and he'd be cheering me on for it."

SYLVESTER STALLONE SCOFFS AT NEPOTISM CRITICS OVER DAUGHTER'S 'TULSA KING' ROLE: 'YOU IDIOT'

"So I saw it as a way to — almost like a conduit to commune with him, wherever he is and may be," James added. "And there's something beautiful about following in those footsteps."

James recalled that Bill had his own way of putting his son’s decision to follow him into acting in perspective.

WATCH: BILL PAXTON'S SON SAYS HE COULD 'LITERALLY HEAR' LATE DAD WHILE TAKING ON HIS WESTERN ROLE

"Dad had this metaphor about if this was 100 years ago, and we were a family of shoemakers or cobblers, my father before me was a shoemaker and his father before him, you'd probably go into the family business and become, hopefully, a good shoemaker," James said. "So I've always held that close."

Before Bill's death, he had been working with McDowell and producer Brad Wyman on the "Last Train to Fortune's" revival with Adam Rifkin as director, but financing repeatedly prevented the project from moving forward. After Bill's death, Rifkin, Wyman and McDowell eventually approached James, who previously said that he hadn't even known about the film while his father was alive.

According to Rifkin, the movie was finally able to secure financing once James signed on.

Bringing the project to fruition also had personal significance for Adam, whose late mother, Michele Rifkin, penned the original script for a PBS screenwriting competition in 1986.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"It was always her son Adam's dream to bring the film to life," James said.

James recalled that Michele had been unable to visit the set as she was bedridden in the hospital during the movie's production. However, the late screenwriter had the opportunity to see James and McDowell in costume when the duo FaceTimed her during filming.

"She told us that when she saw us in costume it was like we had walked right out of her imagination up off the page and into the real world," he remembered. "And that was so touching, and it immediately made me think about my dad in that moment."

"Michele passed away not long after that, and she got to see the finished film before it was released privately, which was amazing, but it made me think all the more about my dad," James said. "Because I know that he … would've wanted us to make this even if he was still around, if they had never got off the ground. He would have been like, ‘James, here, this is your role,’ and so that kind of really made me think of him in that moment in particular."

SCOTT EASTWOOD CREDITS HIS FAMOUS FATHER'S WORK ETHIC FOR MAKING HIM AWARE OF 'BULLS---' IN THE FILM INDUSTRY

Although James was stepping into a role once intended for his father, he said he knew Bill would have wanted him to find his own approach to the character.

"It was totally important for me to create my own version just because I know what Dad would tell me," he said. "And it's tough for me because he was my best friend, so all I wanna do is talk about him and celebrate him, but he goes, 'You're your own actor. You've been studying this. You're a professional.'"

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"I've done a lot of work actually in the past years that he's been gone," James continued. "But I know that he always wanted me to make it my own, and he would be like, 'Don't hitch up on my wagon too much, you'll find it in yourself.' But he would just give me these great acting pieces of advice and wisdom. So I knew that he wouldn't want me to focus on that. He'd say, 'Focus on, it's the character's moment to live, it's Jedediah Dooley's moment to come to life.' So it's not James up there, it's not Bill up there, it's the character."

While Bill encouraged his son to forge his own path as an actor, James recalled that his father was equally determined for his children to develop discipline in other areas of their lives. Along with James, Bill shared daughter Lydia with his wife, Louise Newbury.

"He didn't love it when my sister and I would sleep in too late," James remembered. "He was a bit of a drill sergeant when it came to just getting up and doing something. So he would come in, and I became almost like — it was Pavlovian. As a kid, I became conditioned to hear his footsteps coming down the hall. And if I wasn't sitting up and out of my bed by the time he came in the room, he'd rip the sheets off of me, and he'd go, 'Rise and shine, you're burning daylight out here.'"

"And he just put up the blinds, and it would just flood the room with blinding light and I would freak out a bit," James continued. "But he'd get me going, and so I — even in my half-asleep state — I could jolt awake when I'd hear him coming. Even on the weekends, if he was home, he'd be like, ‘Come on man, get up and do something.’ He wasn't controlling about what that was, but it was about motivating me not to just stay in bed."

James recalled how Bill also wanted his son to have real-life experiences and not define himself solely through acting.

WATCH: BILL PAXTON'S SON RECALLS 'DRILL SERGEANT' DAD RIPPING SHEETS OFF HIM FOR SLEEPING IN

"I used to have a ton of all kinds of odd jobs," James recalled. "I worked in tons of restaurants. I apprenticed as a tile maker. I worked for UPS. I had a lot of really cool experiences. I scooped ice cream, that was my first job. And those were largely thanks to dad encouraging me to do that."

Though James said Bill supported his acting ambitions, he recalled that his father tried to prepare him for the realities of working in Hollywood.

"I would say he was probably more concerned with warning me about all of the pitfalls and the hardships that can fall," James said. "Even somebody as successful as he was in his career, he ran the gamut of every Hollywood experience and every disappointment.

"And he always talked about it's the time between jobs where you really can suffer," he continued. "'The death of a thousand paper cuts.' he would call it. You have to find something that can buoy you between jobs, and you don't put your self-worth in it."

"If anything, he was like, ‘Man if you want to do anything else like, even just as much as this, do that instead,’" James recalled. "He was like, ‘This is a hard thing’ and so if anything, he kind of gave me this extra chip on my shoulder because I was like, 'Well, I'm gonna go, and I'm going to book something and show him.'"

James made his career breakthrough in the USA Network crime thriller drama "Eyewitness," which premiered in October 2016. While speaking with Fox News Digital, James recalled Bill's reaction when he landed the leading role of Lukas Waldenbeck in the series.

"He almost couldn't believe it, but there was this huge sense of relief," James said. "And he called it a ‘real ticket to ride,' as in, it was his way of saying, 'This is a real opportunity. Now you go and show them and stuff. You've done the work to get here.'"

"So that was really cool," he continued. "He saw that right before he passed, which was amazing."

Since starring in "Eyewitness," James has steadily built his acting career with appearances in projects including "Training Day," "Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.," "Tacoma FD" and "The Cleaner." In 2024, he made a cameo in "Twisters," the standalone sequel to his father’s 1996 blockbuster "Twister."

"I still get the whole 'it's Bill Paxton's son' thing, but I have over 45 acting credits," James told Fox News Digital. "But I laugh it off. As Dad would say, man it's all just — it's a great experience, and you're on the path."

In "Last Train to Fortune," McDowell's character Cecil Peachtree misses the last train to his new teaching job in the frontier town of Fortune and enlists the help of James' Jedidiah Booley to get him there safely, with the mismatched pair forming an unlikely bond along the way.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

In addition to their long-held plans to co-star in the movie, McDowell and Bill were close friends and neighbors in Ojai, California. James told Fox News Digital that McDowell recently reminded him of a story that illustrated how the "Clockwork Orange" star's friendship with his father extended far beyond Hollywood.

"I grew up in the Ojai Valley, and we've obviously been plagued by a lot of wildfires over the years," he said. "And it was a pretty bad one when I was quite young. I can't recall exactly, it was early 2000s. Malcolm had a property that was kind of up in the hills, backing up against a lot of wildlife, ground, and forest. And the fire was coming up on his property, and he said that he saw Dad show up in full volunteer fireman regalia, like the full suit, ready to fight the fire with Malcolm.

"And there's a great photo that Kelly, Malcolm's wife, sent to me of the two of them," he continued. "We'll have to track it down because it's great. It's them, you know, they took a quick picture as they were fighting the fire and protecting the Ojai Valley. So I loved the thought of them working together on something outside of film, in real life."

WATCH: BILL PAXTON WARNED SON ABOUT HOLLYWOOD'S 'DEATH OF A THOUSAND PAPER CUTS'

When asked what he believed would make his father most proud of the person he has become, James pointed to his determination to keep going despite the difficult moments he has faced.

"I think he'd be most proud that I have never given up," James said. "I think the perseverance. I think that if our past loved ones can see us at times, they can see our energy or something, they can see us from another place while we're alive, they'd see that there's often like moments of true despair."

"I mean, I would be lying if I said I didn't come close to giving up on a lot of things many times and being like, 'What's the point to keep it going?', but then I realize that's just a wallowing pity party," he continued. "You've got to recognize the blessings and the privilege and keep it going. He's like, ‘I set this up for you.' And so I just want him to know that I'm always gonna honor what he gave me."

"Last Train to Fortune" arrives on VOD Nov. 6th

item.title: Dems pivot from ‘affordability’ pitch to DHS probe threats after midterm wins
item.description: Robert Garcia and other Democrats campaigned on affordability but pivoted to subpoenas and Trump investigations after winning, Fox News Digital found.
item.content:encoded:
Several prominent Democrats who ran on an "affordability" message were largely silent when pressed by Fox News Digital on their sudden pivot to foreshadowing investigations into the Trump administration, including in many cases its immigration enforcement efforts.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to lead the House Oversight Committee, responded to Democrats' win Tuesday with a statement: "Lawyer Up", despite having pledged to prioritize household costs alongside government accountability.

Garcia told CNN before the election that "Democratic priorities" would be lowering the cost of "gas, groceries, the mortgage, the rent," alongside combating government corruption.

PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP

In response to a request for comment, a representative for Garcia shared a tweet he posted Wednesday, after his Tuesday "lawyer up" warning, that referenced affordability:

"People can’t afford gas, groceries, and rent because Donald Trump and his family are ripping off the American people and enriching themselves. Taking on corruption is about making life more affordable for working families," Garcia said in the tweet.

Before the election, "Squad" Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., wrote in a PBS-Chicago voters guide that there is "no question that the rising cost of living is the number one issue" for a "working people’s agenda."

After the election, however, her tone appeared to change:

"Noem, Markwayne, Miller, Homan, Bovino, what’s up? Clear your schedule," Ramirez said.

Several respondents pushed back, including one of her stated targets, former Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino.

"Honey, slow your totalitarian roll," Bovino responded on X. "Citizens don’t answer to communists in this country as much as you seem to believe that."

Bovino went on to suggest Ramirez instead relax with a bottle of whiskey from a brand the former immigration official launched upon retirement.

Other respondents also pointed out that Ramirez’ post-election missive didn’t mention her affordability priority:

SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS

"Notice nothing about how she is going to help her constituents but ‘get Trump’," said one.

"So, you guys never really gave a s--- about affordability," added former Energy Department staffer Matt van Swol.

Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J., who now represents the longtime Republican-held seat of former Rep. Rodney Frelinghuysen, made both affordability and immigration policy part of her campaign message.

"We’re going to toss out subpoenas like Mardi Gras beads," Mejia’s first X post Wednesday read.

Rep. Tony Wied, R-Wis., responded it showed Democrats "have no plans to make life better for you," eliciting a response from Mejia in which she dubbed him "Mr. Weird" and only then mentioned an "economy that works for" Americans.

In April, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., released a lengthy statement announcing a "New Affordability Agenda" and highlighting her role on the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ "Lowering Costs Task Force."

On Election Night, Ansari posted: "Thank you Mr. President. Our thank-you will come in January with subpoenas." An ensuing tweet called for the impeachment of War Secretary Pete Hegseth.

On Wednesday, Ansari ultimately posted a policy-related pledge to curtail AI.

Sen. Edward Markey, D-Mass., stated during the midterms that his priorities were "groceries, gas prices energy costs" and the like.

However, his post-election missive remarking on how many "new forests" will need planting for "all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing," instead signaled a priority to investigate tech executives like Elon Musk.

"Affordability," quipped former Virginia Del. Nick Freitas, R-Culpeper, in a reply.

Ramirez, Mejia, Markey and Ansari did not respond to requests for comment on their apparent pivots. Garcia’s representative responded by providing his subsequent post on affordability. Both Garcia and Ramirez had previously identified government accountability and immigration oversight, respectively, as priorities, but their immediate post-election statements emphasized investigations rather than the affordability measures they had highlighted on the campaign trail.

DHS appeared to take the newfound priority in stride in comments to Fox News Digital.

"It is unfortunate that Democrats are more interested in political shenanigans than in governing," said DHS’ top attorney James Percival.

"Rest assured, however, that we are well prepared to deal with this nonsense so Secretary Mullin can continue focusing on protecting the homeland," the counsel said.

A Justice Department spokesperson echoed Percival, saying the agency is "not afraid of threats from Democrats" and assured its staff has followed the law.

"It is no surprise that rather than focus on bringing down costs for Americans, Democrats in Congress are picking up where their weaponization efforts left off when they were last in power," the spokesperson said.

Meanwhile, the White House told Fox News Digital that Trump remains willing to work with Democrats on issues they can collaborate on to help "hardworking Americans."

"If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical-left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

Immigration hawks signaled preparations for what Democrats foreshadowed.

The Mass Deportation Coalition, whose leaders have been critical of Biden-era open-border policies and have asserted that the Trump administration has not done enough on the issue in some areas, told Fox News Digital they are prepared to defend officials amid the onslaught.

"We know what’s coming," said Mass Deportation Coalition leader Mike Howell. "A lot of people are going to be cashing-out and charging patriots expensive legal fees to the most vulnerable."

"We have been through this before and are ready to sacrifice for the patriots who are targeted by weaponized harassment."

Former House Oversight Committee counsel and immigration judge Andrew Arthur said Congress has the prerogative to investigate DHS’ work but added that it may not be what Americans are looking for as a priority.

Citing Ramirez’ mention of Border Czar Tom Homan, Arthur noted that the onetime Obama official long held "positive" ratings from Republicans and Democrats.

"He was commonly viewed as the guy who came in and cleaned things up after Noem left, got things a little bit better. So that's probably not going to be a terribly popular thing," he said.

"This isn't really affordability but anything that shows waste in government technically goes to affordability and it all depends on how willing the media is to accept that talking point," said Arthur, now at the Center for Immigration Studies.

Arthur said DHS can largely proceed as usual with its previously established funding while any investigations take place, adding that much of what Mullin and Trump have done already falls under established law that Congress itself passed.

Referencing the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, Arthur said that, short of "amending the law itself – which they can’t do if [Trump] vetoes it" Democrats can probe and try to paint the agency in a "bad light" over ICE-involved shootings and similar incidents, but that their larger agenda would be buttressed by the INA.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

A 2026 whitepaper by Federal Reserve Bank researchers found elevated "unauthorized" immigration contributed to rising housing costs between 2021 and 2024, estimating that the influx increased home prices by 6.6% and rents by 4.3% in the average metropolitan area.

The researchers attributed the increases to additional housing demand that was not matched by sufficient new construction, lending indirect empirical support to arguments that illegal immigration can have adverse effects on key affordability metrics.

item.title: College football fans face $2,985 hotel nights, $800 tickets and mortgage decisions for Saturday's CFP slate
item.description: From South Bend to Knoxville to Oxford, college football fans face hotel prices topping $2,000 a night and ticket prices reaching four figures.
item.content:encoded:
The biggest weekend of the college football season has led to fans having to make some interesting financial decisions across the country ahead of what is shaping up to be a wild Saturday.

The question is whether you are prepared to spend thousands of dollars that could go towards a down payment on a new vehicle, for a hotel room around college towns that will keep you close to the action, or hundreds on a ticket just to get inside a stadium.

But, let's be honest, some of these games are just too hard to turn down if given the opportunity to attend.

From South Bend to Baton Rouge, all the way to Knoxville or Oxford, and out to Salt Lake City, fans will invade these towns by the truckload to experience one of the biggest weekends in recent memory with so much on the line.

For the hardcore fans, they,ve had a plan over at least the past year. But, for those scratching an itch of FOMO, it's going to cost you this weekend in college towns across America.

And, Notre Dame is the best place to start, where you will need to make a decision on whether paying the mortgage is more important than attending the most nostalgic game of the weekend.

No, I'm not talking about a luxurious night inside a 5-star resort within miles of Notre Dame's campus.

If you were hellbent on staying near the 'Golden Dome', the LaQuinta Inn 'Suites' had you covered for the low-low price of $2,985 per night over Friday and Saturday.

Have you lost your mind? Look, I get wanting to be close to the action, but the price surging is starting to remind me of the Taylor Swift 'Eras Tour'. If you needed a little relief, staying 3.2 miles away from campus in Mishawaka will knock at least $1,500 off your nightly bill, with the fan-favorite 'Country Inn and Suites' averaging $1,185 per night.

Don't worry, though, the continental breakfast will assuredly make it worth the stay. You can't beat powdered eggs and oatmeal to go with that morning coffee.

Here's a tip: go stay in Chicago or Kalamazoo and pay $230 a night, then make the drive to South Bend for kickoff.

CFP RANKINGS: NOTRE DAME FACES SUDDEN DEATH, SEC FEELING GOOD, AND BIG TEN CLOSE TO HITTING THE PANIC BUTTON

Speaking of the actual game, the No. 11 Notre Dame versus No. 1 Miami classic showdown will have fans paying anywhere between $700 to $10,000 just to witness this very important game with massive CFP implications.

Godspeed to those who are trying to hide expenses with their significant other until the next credit card statement hits your inbox.

If the local Super-8 motel is charging $700 per night, you know it's a college football weekend filled with high stakes.

As No. 10 Ole Miss prepares to host No. 2 Georgia on Saturday night in Oxford, those hoping to have a place to lay their head following the important SEC showdown within the town have already spent thousands.

Look, I'm a points guy when it comes to hotels I reserve before a travel weekend, but paying $1,384 per night to stay at the 'Townplace Suites' might cause some friction to significant others who have access to the joint-checking account.

Just stay 25 miles or so outside of town and enjoy a 'Home2Suites' in Batesville, Mississippi for $500 per night, which will save you from a mental breakdown once that payment comes due next month.

LANE KIFFIN FUMES OVER ALABAMA KICKOFF TIME, ACCUSES SEC OF NOT WANTING LSU TO WIN

As for actually attending the Rebels vs. Dawgs game, $250 per ticket is a steal when you think about the magnitude of this one.

Over in Knoxville, Tennessee, those waiting until the last minute were in luck.

The highly-anticipated rivalry game that will see No. 6 Kentucky entering a 'Dark Mode' version of Neyland Stadium on Saturday night to face No. 13 Tennessee.

Luckily for those looking for a place to stay, the comfortable 'Hilton Garden Inn' just eight miles from campus will only cost you $320 a night, and that glorious breakfast is included.

But, getting into the actual game with CFP ramifications for both teams will cost fans anywhere from $353 to $940 to experience this environment that will feel more like a Halloween night in Knoxville.

My advice? If you can afford it, go enjoy the spooky night with 100,000 fans wearing their favorite black Tennessee decor, along with a few thousand Kentucky fans decked out in their best blue.

Luckily for LSU and Alabama fans making the trek to Tiger Stadium for the Saturday afternoon SEC showdown, the afternoon kickoff time that everyone seems to be complaining about will actually pay-off for those looking for a reasonable nightly rate.

From anywhere between $300 to $500 per night, you can stay within six miles of LSU's campus.

And, you can get into this game for around $240, which is a steal for this rivalry game that will be played for the last time on an annual basis this weekend.

As for the 'Holy War' that will see No. 9 BYU face No. 3 Utah in what is the second-most intriguing game of the weekend, it will cost more to get into the actual Big 12 showdown than what it could take to stay the night.

A $381 'get in' price will be well-worth the cost of admission for this one, even if ESPN picked the wrong kickoff time, with a 10 a.m. local time start.

If you are attending the No. 7 Texas vs. No. 18 Missouri matchup in Columbia, the $500 per night accommodations will only have you paying out extraordinary prices on Friday night, thanks to the wonderful 11 a.m. kickoff time.

But, it will cost you anywhere between $150 to $597 to get into this sneaky-good SEC showdown that will see Arch Manning try to keep the Longhorns rolling after the win over Ole Miss last week, while Austin Simmons can keep the Tigers within striking distance of the College Football Playoff.

Alright, if you've been following my advice this season on travel expenses, you’re already ahead of those that don't.

Sure, I have a weird fascination with ticket prices and hotel accommodations. But, I hope you have used my quirky investigative mind to your advantage and you enjoy this monster slate of college football without breaking the bank.

Let's have ourselves a weekend, as we inch closer to conference championship games that will bring this regular season to an end.
